Jack S. Bell , BM, BCh; Edward Nicol , MD; Vinod Venugopal , MD; Liam Mullen, PhD; Laurence Tidbury , PhD; Matthew Shaw , PhD; Campbell Rogers , MD; Sarah Mullen , MBT; Bjarne Linde Nørgaard, PhD; Jonathon Leipsic , MD; Jonathan R. Weir-McCall , PhD; Timothy A. Fairbairn , PhD, on behalf of the FISH&CHIPS Investigators*

BACKGROUND: The diagnostic value of coronary computed tomography angiography–derived fractional flow reserve (FFR-CT) in stable coronary artery disease is well established. The prognostic value of predicting future cardiovascular events is less clear, as studies are limited by small populations, variable measurement points, composite outcomes, and short follow-up.

The addition of FFR-CT improved discrimination for MI or cardiovascular death compared with a risk factor and stenosis severity model (C index, 0.783; ∆C index, 0.012; P<0.001). An FFR-CT value of 0.67 defined the optimal cutoff for risk of future cardiovascular events. Distalvessel FFR-CT was associated with outcomes similar to stenosis-specific FFR-CT. Stenosis-specific and distal-vessel FFRCT discordance was common (36.4%), but when stenosis-specific FFR-CT was normal, event rates were low (1.5% at 3 years for MI or cardiovascular death).

CONCLUSIONS:FFR-CT is associated with the individual outcomes of MI, cardiovascular death, and all-cause death independent of risk factors and stenosis severity, with lower FFR-CT values associated with worse outcomes. Reduced and severely reduced FFR-CT have the strongest association with future cardiovascular events, with a value of 0.67 defining the optimal risk threshold.

blocks.sourceText: (CCTA) is a first-line investigation for suspected stable coronary artery disease (CAD) with excellent sensitivity for detecting coronary plaque. Historically, CCTA was limited in relating a coronary stenosis to flow reduction, and therefore angina symptoms, often requiring downstream functional investigations or invasive coronary angiography. This limitation has been addressed with CCTA-derived fractional flow reserve (FFR-CT), which uses principles of computational fluid dynamics to estimate flow in the coronary tree. FFR-CT has been validated against invasive FFR,1–3 and trials have shown that a diagnostic strategy incorporating FFR-CT reduces the rate of unnecessary invasive coronary angiography at a neutral cost.4–6 Therefore, FFR-CT is recommended for use in the chest pain pathway as a diagnostic aid to CCTA.7

What Is New?• Coronary computed tomography angiography fractional flow reserve (FFR-CT) predicts the individual outcomes of myocardial infarction (MI), cardiovascular death, all-cause death, and revascularization independent of clinical risk factors and coronary artery stenosis severity. • There is a continuum of risk with decreasing FFRCT, and a binary stenosis-specific threshold of 0.67 identifies individuals at increased risk for future MI and cardiovascular death.

Akin to invasive FFR, FFR-CT may provide prognostic information for predicting future major adverse cardiovascular events.8,9 However, the evidence to date is based on small numbers, composite outcomes, or a limited follow-up period. It therefore remains uncertain whether

• By directly comparing stenosis-specific and distalvessel FFR-CT, we show similar discrimination for future cardiovascular events, with stenosis-specific FFR-CT having a stronger association with MI and cardiovascular death and distal-vessel FFR-CT with all-cause death.

FISH&CHIPS was a multicenter, retrospective, quasi-experimental observational cohort study of 90 553 patients, investigating the impact of a national FFR-CT implementation program on patient cardiovascular outcomes and cardiac tests. The study design has6

been reported previously. In brief, all patients ≥18 years, investigated with CCTA for suspected CAD from 27 English hospitals between 2017 and 2020, were included. The decision to send a CCTA for FFR-CT analysis was at the discretion of the clinical team. Clinical management was informed following the availability of the FFR-CT result via a written report and online access to the patient-specific anatomical and physiological 3D reconstruction.6

FFR-CT analysis (HeartFlow Inc, Mountain View, CA) reported distal FFR-CT in the main epicardial vessels and stenosisspecific FFR-CT 2 cm distal to a stenosis ≥30% in any vessel ≥1.8 mm. When a stenosis-specific FFR-CT value was in the distal segment of the vessel, it was used as both the distal and stenosis-specific result. Patients were categorized on the basis of the lowest FFR-CT value: ≤0.50 (severely reduced), 0.51 to 0.70 (reduced), 0.71 to 0.80 (borderline), and >0.80 (normal).

Continuous variables are reported as mean (±SD) or median (interquartile range) and categorical as number (percent). Between-group differences were assessed by ANOVA for continuous variable and a Cochran-Armitage trend test for categorical differences, with the “no stenosis-specific value” group representing the category with the least disease. Time to first

event was calculated using Kaplan-Meier methodology from the time of the CCTA. Cox proportional regression was used to determine the univariable hazard ratio (HR) for individual clinical outcomes post FFR-CT, and the proportional hazardassumptions were tested using Shoenfeld residuals. Fine-Grey modeling was performed to account for competing risks where necessary. Multivariable Cox regression models were used to adjust for patient cardiovascular risk factors (age, sex, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia) and the Coronary Artery Disease Reporting and Data System (CAD-RADS) score. Models were developed to determine the performance of baseline risk factors and demographics (model 1), +CAD-RADS score (model 2), +FFR-CT (model 3), and +delta FFR-CT (model 4) for the combined end point of MI and cardiovascular death. Model performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis with Harrell’s C statistic and the Akaike information criterion with the Brier score as a measure of model calibration. FFR-CT was entered into an adjusted multivariable model as a continuous variable to provide an adjusted HR (aHR) per 0.01 unit decrease in stenosis-specific FFR-CT. Incremental Predictive Value Over Established Risk Factors

The addition of coronary stenosis severity (CAD-RADS) to a model containing clinical risk factors (age, sex, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia) showed improved discrimination for nonfatal MI or cardiovascular death (C index, 0.771 versus 0.758; P=0.007). Including stenosis-

specific FFR-CT further improved discrimination (C index, 0.783 versus 0.771; P<0.001) compared with the clinical risk factor and CAD-RADS model (Figure 3). Addition of delta FFR-CT (≥0.12 cutoff) did not improve discrimination (C index, 0.782 versus 0.783; P=0.72) (Figure 3).
FFR-CT as a Continuum for Predicting Future Events

Entering stenosis-specific FFR-CT as a continuous variable into a multivariable model adjusted for clinical risk factors and CAD-RADS showed a significant relationship to MI (aHR, 1.04 per 0.1-unit decrease [95% CI, 1.01–1.15]; P<0.001), cardiovascular mortality (aHR, 1.08 [95% CI, 1.008–1.73]; P=0.03), and revascularization (aHR, 1.006 [95% CI, 1.003–1.009]; P<0.001) but not for all-cause mortality (aHR, 1.50 [95% CI, 0.16–1.56]; P=0.23). Comparison of Stenosis-Specific and DistalVessel FFR-CT

Models using stenosis-specific and distal-vessel FFRCT categories were similar for discriminating individual cardiovascular outcomes. Stenosis-specific models had better fits for MI and revascularization, while distal models had a better fit for all-cause mortality (Table 2). When stenosis-specific FFR-CT was negative, cardiovascular event rates were low (1.4% at 3 years for nonfatal MI and cardiovascular death combined). In this group, distal FFR-CT values were concordant (ie, negative) in 63.4% of cases and discordant in 36.4% (35.1% borderline, 1.3% reduced, 0% severely reduced). This large multicenter study is the first to show that FFRCT stratifies risk for the individual outcomes of MI, cardiovascular death, all-cause death, and revascularization at 3 years. Importantly, this is incremental to clinical risk factors and coronary stenosis severity. A risk continuum exists, as lower FFR-CT values are associated with incrementally worse prognosis, with an optimum stenosisspecific threshold of 0.67 for defining increased risk of future cardiac events. Stenosis-specific and distal-vessel FFR-CT models performed equivalently in discriminating outcomes, although stenosis-specific models had better fits for MI and revascularization.

The largest previous study, from the Danish ADVANCE registry, showed that a positive FFR-CT was associated with an increased risk of all-cause death and MI combined out to 7 years of follow-up.17 Our study reports a larger population with 10 times more clinical

events, allowing us to determine that FFR-CT is associated with the individual outcomes of MI, cardiovascular death, and all-cause death independent of clinical risk factors and diameter of stenosis. The incremental predictive capacity of adding FFRCT to coronary stenosis adds to the debate around the prognostic relevance of myocardial ischemia compared with anatomical CAD severity. Interestingly, delta FFR-CT, the translesional gradient across a stenosis, akin to pull-back pressure gradient on invasive FFR, did not further improve model performance. Delta FFR-CT has been shown to improve identification of ischemic lesions and be the strongest predictor of future cardiac events, but these studies did not control for clinical risk factors.20,21 There is a gradient of risk, as lower FFR-CT values increase the likelihood of all of the individual outcomes. Clinical guidelines recommend a binary cutoff point at ≤0.80 for distinguishing normal from abnormal. This approach neglects important information about patient risk of future adverse events, which may be useful to inform patient-doctor decisions concerning the risk-benefit of revascularization but also the intensity of medical management. The association of FFRCT subgroups and future events was strongest for MI, where all positive stenosis-specific FFR-CT subgroups (≤0.80) were associated with MI, with subgroups ≤0.70 associated with around 3 times increased MI risk, even xxx xxx, 2026

A borderline “gray zone” category has been established in invasive FFR and FFR-CT, recognizing lower comparative diagnostic accuracy, measurement variabilities, and lower evidence of treatment benefit.22–24 The exact range of the “gray zone” and how to interpret this category for patient management are frequently debated. Our data show that a borderline stenosisspecific FFR-CT (0.71–0.80) was associated with increased risk of future MI and revascularization but not survival. FFR-CT≤0.70 is associated with increased risk for cardiovascular and all-cause death, identifying those at highest risk for whom treatment may have the greatest potential to impact clinical outcomes. Borderline distal values, however, had no association with future cardiovascular events other than revascularization. Interpreting FFR-CT as a continuum for risk of future cardiac events would seem most appropriate. However, we did identify a stenosis-specific FFR-CT cutoff at 0.67 for the prediction of nonfatal MI or cardiovascular death. Our observations raise the question as to whether distal vessel FFR-CT values should be reported, as the models based on distal-vessel and stenosis-specific FFR-CT perform similarly. The risk of a “don’t report distal” approach is that potentially important patientspecific information is not used, as reduced and severely reduced distal-vessel values do have an association with future cardiovascular events and all-cause death. This is corroborated by invasive studies showing that distal FFR in the 3 main epicardial vessels predicts major adverse cardiovascular events.27 Distal values may reflect plaque burden over the entire epicardial coronary artery rather than specific obstructive stenoses, with lower values

of total plaque volume across the coronary tree in predicting major adverse cardiovascular events, not just stenosis severity or presence of ischemia.28 However, it is challenging to disentangle the impact of distal FFR-CT from an upstream stenosis-specific FFR-CT, and here, discordance analyses may offer insight. In the instance of a negative stenosis-specific FFR-CT (>0.80) there was a positive distal FFR-CT in 36.4% of cases, but only 1.3% were reduced (≤0.7), with the rest borderline (0.71–0.80). The borderline group had the same cardiovascular event rates as the normal group, but cardiovascular event rates were significantly higher in the small group of patients with reduced distal values. Borderline distal values can occur in the absence of upstream plaque due to other mechanisms such as myocardial bridging, natural vessel tapering, and insufficient spatial resolution in small vessels.29 This may partly explain the absence of incremental prognostic benefit. Thus, it is reasonable to use stenosis-specific values alone for guiding the diagnosis, prognosis, and management strategy when the stenosis FFR-CT is positive.

When there is distal and stenosis-specific discordance, in a small number of patients, distal FFR-CT provides potentially useful prognostic information when reduced ≤0.70. Interestingly, a subgroup of patients with distal stenoses in the main epicardial vessels had the highest rates of cardiovascular and all-cause mortality, with similar rates of MI and revascularization as the reduced FFR-CT group. This is a hypothesis-generating finding that raises questions around the dogma that only proximal disease is “prognostic.”30,31

As an observational study, the FFR-CT results likely influenced downstream patient management, especially revascularization. Despite this, we observe associations between FFR-CT and clinical outcomes. MI inherently spans several entities, including early events before revascularization, procedure-related events, and late events. Distinguishing periprocedural (type 4) events from post xxx xxx, 2026

revascularization events that occurred during the same admission is not possible with our dataset. Data were not available for plaque burden, smoking status, and family history, which may be relevant for predicting cardiovascular outcomes. It has yet to be determined whether FFRCT offers incremental prognostic value over total plaque burden.32,33 Future work should aim to integrate FFR-CT and clinical risk factors alongside other CCTA markers of risk, such as quantified plaque volumes and pericoronary fat attenuation, to develop improved personalized risk models for patients to guide preventative care.28,34

FFR-CT predicts the clinical outcomes of MI, cardiovascular death, all-cause death, and revascularization independent of patient risk factors and diameter stenosis, with a gradient of risk where reduced andseverely reduced FFRCT values are linked to worse survival.
